reasoning.notes: Most decisions rest on specific, mostly correct inference: players read the opponent's Obsession from retained cards, track which cards will come back after the swaps, and estimate the opponent's madness icons to contest or deny the bonus. Many picks list both possible returning cards and compare exact tide scores, which is what the designer's notes call for.

evidence.quote: The opponent kept Shore*-1 and took Idols*-2, so they have at least 2 icons. If I take Stars-2 instead, they are forced to take Stars*-2, reach 3 icons against my 1, and win the 4-point madness bonus.
evidence.shows: Estimates the opponent's hidden icon count and drafts to deny the madness bonus.

evidence.quote: The opponent sits at 6 madness, so they will probably take the plain Shore-3 and pass me Deep*-2.
evidence.shows: Predicts the opponent's pick from their madness limit and builds a full outcome table. The prediction was right.

evidence.quote: The opponent keeps Stars-4 and Stars*-1, so Stars is very likely their Obsession again... denying them that matters more than anything else in this hand.
evidence.shows: Infers the hidden Obsession from retained cards and hate-drafts while behind.

evidence.quote: By tracking the swaps, seat 1 has drafted one unknown card plus Ruins-1 and Ruins-3. That makes Ruins their likely Obsession.
evidence.shows: Reconstructs the opponent's face-down picks from the passed hands.

planning.notes: Players set up picks several rounds ahead: they take one card of a pair now because the other will return, count on the opponent ignoring a suit, and retain cards to shape the next tide's Obsession. They plan across tides to stay under the madness threshold of 9, most clearly in match 2.

evidence.quote: the opponent is likely building Shore, given their two retained Shore cards, so they probably won't take Ruins-2.
evidence.shows: A multi-round plan that relies on the opponent's behaviour. It worked: Ruins-2 came back at turn 33 for 4 Ruins.

evidence.quote: My madness is at 6, and I lose at 9, so I can only take 2 madness icons in tide 3. A plain card keeps that margin.
evidence.shows: Retains a plain card to plan around the threshold. The player keeps to this madness budget through turns 28-34.

evidence.quote: If I take Deep-1 now, the opponent takes one of those two, and my forced ... pick is the other. That adds one icon, so I end at 8.
evidence.shows: Plans the remaining three picks of the tide around the swap order and the madness cap.

evidence.quote: My last card will be whichever of Idols-1 or Deep-1 my opponent passes back. With Stars-3, either of those gives me 4 different suits.
evidence.shows: Secures the 4-suit bonus by planning around the forced last card.

luck.notes: The deals set which suits could become a strong Obsession, for example seat 2 getting four Stars in match 2 tide 1, and the final margins were only 4, 1 and 3 points. Choices still shifted the results, but the deal decided part of the outcome.

evidence.quote: Taking Stars*-2 gives me four Stars, my Obsession. That scores 10 × 2 = 20 points
evidence.shows: A favourable deal gave a 4-card Obsession set and a 6-point tide lead in a game decided by 1 point.

evidence.quote: I'm making Ruins my Obsession because I hold three Ruins in my opening hand.
evidence.shows: The opening hand dealt drives the choice of Obsession.

weak_spots.what: Took Shore-1 (+6) instead of hate-drafting Ruins-2, saying denial was worth 'about the same 6 points... only if Ruins is really their Obsession'. Seat 2 had retained Ruins-1 and Ruins*-1, so Ruins was almost certain. Ruins-2 would be their 4th Ruins, worth 20 against 12 (8 points), so denying it was worth more in a game lost by 4.

Kept the same openly signalled Obsession (Shore, with Shore cards retained) in every tide and never bluffed or used a decoy suit, which invited hate-drafting. A less obvious retain or Obsession was possible.

summary: Winning takes real reasoning and planning: players inferred Obsessions from retained cards, tracked swaps to predict returning cards, raced for the madness bonus, and planned around the 9 threshold. Bluffing and decoy drafts never appeared, and open retained cards make Obsessions easy to read; hiding retained cards or rewarding deception more would make the game demand more.
